decided: Option (b): cmd/shortfall/go.mod drops its three first-party replace directives (the core, adapters/query/promql, adapters/query/sql) so `go install github.com/NightWatchEng/shortfall/cmd/shortfall@<version>` works, and the release trigger moves from the root `v*` tag (wave 1) to the `cmd/shortfall/v*` tag (wave 3) via goreleaser's monorepo.tag_prefix. The CLI is therefore built only at the point where every module it requires is already tagged, published and resolvable, and where the requires bump naming that version has already landed.
why: Both premises that made this bead a genuine dilemma have since expired. The repository is public (2026-09-01), and all sixteen v0.2.0 tags resolve from proxy.golang.org — verified from an empty module with default config: `go get` of the core, promql and sql at v0.2.0 all succeed, so the 'no GOPRIVATE, nothing published, the release build cannot reach the graph at all' objection recorded in CONTRIBUTING no longer holds. Verified empirically, not by reasoning: with the three replaces dropped and go.sum tidied, `GOWORK=off CGO_ENABLED=0 go build` of cmd/shortfall — goreleaser's exact build conditions — compiles against the published modules and the binary runs. test/modgraph's own TestEveryFirstPartyRequireIsReplacedLocally doc comment predicted this exact moment: it calls itself 'a deliberate ratchet on the CURRENT posture, not a permanent law of the repository... once the tag waves in CONTRIBUTING have run, dropping a replace becomes the correct move rather than a defect (it is the tracked path to a working `go install`), and this test is expected to be revisited in that change'. The waves have run. What remains is not a resolution problem but an ordering one: release.yml fires on the root `v*` tag, which is wave 1, so without the replaces a v0.3.0 build would compile the CLI against the previously published core and ship a binary labelled v0.3.0 containing v0.2.0 library code. Moving the trigger to wave 3 is what makes the dropped replaces honest rather than merely convenient — the tag that triggers the release is the tag whose tree names the versions being built.
cost_if_wrong: Two costs, both accepted. (1) The CLI release now cuts on the wave-3 tag instead of wave-1, so a release where the operator tags the core and stops produces no binaries at all — a visible, self-announcing failure (no release assets) rather than a silent wrong one, which is the direction to fail in. (2) Bumping cmd/shortfall/go.mod's three requires to the new version becomes a mandatory release step rather than an irrelevant one, and skipping it ships a correctly-labelled binary built from stale library code. That is the dangerous failure, so it is not left to the checklist: test/modgraph is changed from enforcing a local replace to enforcing that cmd/shortfall's first-party requires name a real published version, and CONTRIBUTING's wave list carries the bump as an ordered step. The inverse error — the status quo — is that the idiomatic Go install path stays broken on a now-public repository, which is the first thing a new adopter tries and the last thing they will file an issue about.
alternatives: (a) Keep the replaces, ship release archives only, record it as deliberate — rejected: it was the right call while the repo was private and nothing was published, and both of those facts have changed. Nothing now pays for the broken install path.

(b-variant) Keep the root v* trigger and give goreleaser a second modfile (GOFLAGS=-modfile=go.release.mod) carrying the replaces, so the committed go.mod is install-clean while the release still builds the working tree — rejected: it buys back wave-1 releases at the price of a second go.mod/go.sum pair inside cmd/shortfall whose drift from the real one is invisible until a release is already wrong, and test/modgraph would have to learn about a modfile no adopter ever sees.

(c) Drop the replaces and vendor cmd/shortfall's first-party deps — rejected, and worth recording why it does not do what the bead assumed: `go install pkg@version` builds in module-aware mode and ignores vendor directories entirely, so vendoring cannot help the install path at all. It would serve only the release build, by committing a copy of first-party code that has to be re-vendored every release — strictly more work than (b) for a strictly worse result.

Order the tag waves so every dependency tag exists before the root v* tag triggers the release — rejected as impossible rather than undesirable: the root v* tag IS both wave 1 and the release trigger, so no ordering of the existing waves can put the core's own tag before itself.
scope: cmd/shortfall/go.mod and go.sum (the three replaces and the resulting sum entries); .goreleaser.yaml (monorepo.tag_prefix); .github/workflows/release.yml (the tag filter only — job structure, permissions and pinned action SHAs unchanged); test/modgraph (the replace ratchet, narrowed rather than deleted); and the docs that state the old posture: README.md, CONTRIBUTING.md (the `go install` paragraph and the Releases wave list), docs/quickstart.md, docs/internal/go-public-checklist.md. No change to the CLI's source, to any library module, or to what the core module publishes. Gate surface is in scope here because workspace-47f's acceptance criteria is explicitly about the release pipeline, which .warden/skills-policy.md 'Forbidden paths' permits for a tracked item about CI, stated in the PR body.
